exit_trigger: Evidence of moat erosion: loss of customer qualifications, sustained pricing pressure, or share loss to rivals; Management failure: value-destroying acquisitions, buybacks at inflated prices, or dishonest reporting; Structural decline in end-market demand that the business cannot offset; Price above 1.5x a conservatively re-estimated intrinsic value, with the gap persistent; A much higher-conviction opportunity requiring capital
rationale: I own this one, and I'm down 21.8% since August at $886.815. A lower price is not a reason to sell a business whose moat is intact; it's the market offering me the same company for less. What I can verify says the economics are good: a 5-year average ROE of 30.6%, debt-to-equity of 0.497, and 5-year average owner earnings of about $413 million against a market cap of about $6.5 billion. The snapshot's intrinsic value of $1,271.73 a share rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, so I treat that 45.5% margin of safety as generous and not as gospel. I keep the shares and don't add until I can see the earnings history and management record this snapshot leaves out.

exit_trigger: Evidence of eroding pricing power: rising markdowns or falling full-price sell-through; Sustained decline in brand relevance and comparable sales; Management capital allocation failures, such as poor acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices; Debt-funded expansion that breaks the zero-leverage profile; Price above 1.5x a conservatively re-estimated intrinsic value
rationale: I own this one, 10 shares at $128.38, and it is down about 17% in 97 days. A price decline by itself does not worry me; a broken moat would. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 34.6% and a debt-to-equity of 0.0, which is the kind of economics I like, and a market cap of about $11.7 billion clears my size bar. The model's $347 intrinsic value rests on 8% growth held for ten years and a 5% discount rate, so I treat it with real skepticism. Apparel is fashion-driven, and the snapshot gives me nothing on pricing power, comparable sales, or management, so I could not verify the brand moat. I keep the position at its current size, add nothing until I can verify the brand is holding, and I will sell if the evidence says pricing power is eroding.

exit_trigger: Evidence of manufacturer franchise erosion or a shift to direct-to-consumer sales that bypasses dealers; Service and parts profitability deteriorating structurally; Management making large acquisitions at peak prices or taking on leverage above debt-to-equity 0.5; Price above 1.5x intrinsic value, persistently; Evidence of accounting problems or dishonesty
rationale: I own 6 shares of Penske Automotive, bought at $216.765 and now at $213.27, down 1.61% after 97 days, which is noise and not a thesis change. The snapshot gives me a 5-year average ROE of 23.8%, debt-to-equity of 0.39, and an owner-earnings-based value of about $259.62 a share against a $213.27 price, a margin of safety of 17.85%. That clears my 15% bar, but not by a wide margin, and the valuation assumes zero growth at a 5% discount rate. I also cannot verify from this snapshot the 10-year earnings record, the CEO's tenure, the moat statistics, or the insider and 13F activity. Dealers are a competitive, cyclical business, and the moat is more scale and service than a true franchise. So I keep what I own, I do not add on this evidence, and I would add only if the price fell further or the missing checks came back clean.

exit_trigger: Evidence that industrial customers are switching on price alone, eroding the service and availability advantage; Sustained decline in ROE well below 15% outside a cyclical trough; Management makes value-destroying acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices; Discovery of a restatement or dishonest disclosure; Price exceeding 1.5x a conservatively recalculated intrinsic value, persistently
rationale: We own this one, bought 17 days ago at $120.05, and it sits at $120.64, so nothing has happened yet and nothing should. This is a distributor of industrial supplies, a business I can describe in two paragraphs, and the numbers in front of me are respectable: a five-year average ROE of 20.03%, debt-to-equity of 0.35, and a market cap of about $6.7 billion. The snapshot's intrinsic value of $157.18 rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, which is more generous than I would like. A 23% margin of safety on those inputs is therefore thinner than it looks. I'll keep the shares and add nothing until I can verify ten years of earnings and the management record, neither of which is in this filing data. If the moat turns out to be a price-competitive commodity channel rather than sticky customer relationships, I'll admit the error early.

exit_trigger: Evidence of brand pricing power eroding, such as sustained share loss or forced price cuts; Technology shift (e.g., heat pumps) that erodes the core water-heater franchise and requires costly rebuilding; Management destroying value through large acquisitions or buybacks at inflated prices; Price exceeding 1.5x intrinsic value with the gap persisting
rationale: I own A. O. Smith, so the question is whether to keep it, and I'm keeping it. It makes water heaters and boilers, a product people replace when it breaks and buy through plumbers who stick with the brand they trust. The snapshot shows a five-year average ROE of 23.7% and a debt-to-equity of 0.08, which is the kind of return on capital without leverage that I like to see. At $64.98 against an owner-earnings value of $95.72, the margin of safety is about 32%, well above my 15% bar, though the 5% discount rate and 8% growth cap deserve some humility. We've held only 20 days, and I can't verify ten years of earnings or the CEO's tenure from this snapshot, so I'm not adding. I'll sit tight and let time work.

exit_trigger: Evidence that brand pricing power is eroding, such as price cuts needed to hold volume; Management destroys value through large overpriced acquisitions or dishonest reporting; Price rising above 1.5x intrinsic value with the gap persisting; A far better opportunity at much higher conviction
rationale: We own 12 shares, bought two weeks ago at $103.57 and now up about 2%, so the only question is whether to keep them. I do. This is a maker of paints, sealants and coatings that people buy by name, and I can explain it in two paragraphs. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE near 22.9% and a margin of safety of about 20.9% against a $133.59 intrinsic value, which clears my 15% bar. But the snapshot does not give me a 10-year earnings record, CEO tenure, or the Treasury yield for my earnings-yield check, and a debt-to-equity of 0.003 looks too low to take at face value. So I hold what I have, I don't pound the table, and I add only if the price falls with the moat intact or the missing checks come back clean.

exit_trigger: Evidence that returns on equity are regressing toward market averages, indicating the moat is not durable; Loss of cost or scale advantage to imports or new competitors, or a structural shift away from the business's main end markets; Capital allocation failure such as overpriced acquisitions or dishonest reporting by management; Price reaching well above 1.5x a conservatively re-derived intrinsic value, with the gap persisting; Discovery that debt is understated or untagged in the reported 0.0 debt-to-equity
rationale: I own this one, bought a week ago at 54.285 and up 1.45% since, so the question is whether I keep it, and I do, but with my eyes open. The numbers on the page are good: a 5-year average ROE of 29.3%, debt-to-equity reported at 0.0, and owner earnings averaging about $646 million against a $6.1 billion market cap. But that $168.53 intrinsic value rests on an 8% growth rate and a 5% discount rate, and I would not bet the farm on a margin of safety that wide; I discount it heavily. My real worry is whether a metals processor has a moat or merely a good run, and the snapshot gives me no evidence on pricing power, cost position, earnings history or management. I will hold the position at its current size, add nothing until those gaps are filled, and sell if the evidence shows a commodity business with no edge.

exit_trigger: Exit now: the position fails my circle-of-competence and moat tests, and the gain so far is not a reason to keep a business I cannot underwrite; Would reconsider only if a verified ten-year earnings record, ROIC above 15% and a documented durable customer lock-in become available and the price still offers at least a 15% margin of safety
rationale: I own 16 shares, bought at $83.50 three days ago and now showing a 9.71% gain, and I have to be honest with myself about why I own them. The numbers in front of me are tidy: a 19.1% five-year average ROE, debt-to-equity of 0.086, and a 20.6% margin of safety on a zero-growth owner-earnings value. But numbers are not a moat. I cannot tell you with confidence what radio-frequency chips will look like in ten years, and this is an industry where the product must be redesigned every cycle. The snapshot gives me no ten-year earnings record, no customer concentration, no ROIC and no management history, so I cannot verify the criteria I demand. A cheap-looking price on a business I cannot describe with certainty is the kind of mistake I have made before, so I would take the quick gain and wait for a pitch in my sweet spot.
